pronunciation.ipaLabel: Conventional reading — Egyptian vocalisation not attested

phonemes.desc: Written qbḥ.t; conventionally vocalised “Kebechet”. The root qbḥ means “cool, fresh”.
Daughter of Anubis, the snake-goddess of purification water.

pronunciation.note: Her name is a promise: the cool water that quenches the thirst of the dead. The final -t marks the feminine, as in most Egyptian goddess-names.

domains.title: Goddess of Purification, the Cool Water of Offerings
domains.subtitle: The Serpent Daughter of Anubis
domains.lead: Qbḥt — Kebechet — is the gentlest of the death-gods’ company: Anubis’ daughter, who takes serpent form and brings the cool, fresh water of purification to the dead. Where her father presides over the weighing, she attends to the washing — the goddess whose element, water, cleanses what the tomb cannot.

cards.name: The Purifying Snake
cards.desc: In serpent form she moves through the embalming tent, her coolness the antidote to decay’s heat.

cards.name: Daughter of Anubis
cards.desc: Child of the embalmer-god; she extends his craft from wrapping to refreshing.

cards.name: The Cool Water
cards.desc: Her name means “cooling”; the libation water she pours revives the dead’s senses.

cards.name: Guardian of the Embalmers
cards.desc: Present at every stage of the wbt-ritual: the purification that precedes mummification.

mythology.lead: Kebechet belongs to the small, precise company of Egyptian funerary deities whose work is a single gesture done perfectly. Her mythology is her function: the cooling of the dead. In the Pyramid Texts she already appears beside her father Anubis, refreshing the king’s flesh with the water that flows in the beyond’s own divine Nile.

myths.title: The Refresher of the King
myths.text: The oldest utterances name Kebechet among the court of the embalming gods: she who ‘refreshes’ the king’s heart, whose cool water runs in the celestial Nile. The afterlife of the Pyramid Texts is a place of thirsts quenched — Kebechet is the goddess holding the cup.

myths.title: The Washing Before the Wrapping
myths.text: The mortuary liturgy divides into the water-rites and the bandage-rites, and Kebechet presides over the first. Before Anubis could wrap, Kebechet had to cool — the purification that made the body fit to be eternal. The ritual texts address her directly as ‘ Kebechet who is upon her father’s lake’.

myths.title: The Beneficent Snake
myths.text: Egypt’s serpent-goddesses divide between the deadly (Meretseger, the fiery Eye) and the beneficent; Kebechet is the gentlest of the second company. Her serpent form is coolness itself — the reptile of the water’s edge, at home in the inundation’s margin where freshness collects.

The embalming tent stood symbolically at the edge of the sacred lake where the gods washed; Kebechet is its personification. In vignettes of the judgement hall she appears beside the scales’ lake, ensuring the water of the test is cool, clean, and truthful.
myths.title: Her Father’s Lake

lore.syncretism: Kebechet absorbed into the greater purification-cycles — identified with the inundation’s first water and with the serpent-forms of Wadjet in her gentle aspect. She is sometimes doubled with Qebehsenuef, the falcon-son of Horus of the canopic jars — the two ‘cool’ divinities of the embalming company.
lore.culturalLegacy: Small as her cult was, she is indispensable to the completeness of Egyptian funerary religion: the theology that remembered to quench the dead’s thirst. Her image — the water-pouring serpent — appears on Late Period stelae from Akhmim to Thebes, and modern studies of embalming cite her as the water-rites’ divine warrant.
lore.extendedMeditation: Qbḥt: four consonants that mean coolness. In a religion of desert and flood, she is the moment between them — the fresh margin. Her restoration needs no ornament; the name itself is a draught of water offered to anyone who reads it aloud.

sources.name: Book of the Dead vignettes (purification scenes)

lore.archaeology: No temple of her own is known — her cult was served within Anubis’ — but her stelae and amulets, the serpent pouring from a jar, are widespread in Late Period material. The embalming caches of Saqqara place her among the gods whose names guaranteed the rite.
lore.cult: Her ‘cult’ was the mortuary water-rite itself: every libation poured for the dead was hers. Priests of the embalming guild invoked her at the washing; families pouring water at tombs addressed her without knowing her name.
lore.iconography: A serpent with a woman’s head, or a woman with serpent’s head, pouring water from a jar; sometimes simply a snake rearing beside the embalmer’s table. Her colour is the blue-green of fresh water on desert stone.
lore.reception: Greek visitors to the necropolises recorded the water-pouring serpent without separating Kebechet from Wadjet; modern Egyptology restored her distinct place through the ritual papyri. She remains the emblem of the small gods — the ones whose whole theology is one merciful act.
